data.title: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum
data.description:
Schools are scrambling after Google said Tuesday that education leaders need to either accept some AI in classrooms or lose access to its search engine.  

School officials trying to push back on an encroaching AI are in a bind. The tech giant dominates search online, and it didn’t give much time for districts to make their decisions.

District leaders say a fight would be a big undertaking, but some may be up to the challenge, especially as public outcry after the announcement grows. 

Google announced that early next year its Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will automatically be turned off for school districts and administrators will have to choose to opt into the features. However, the company said Search and AI are “deeply integrated”, and it will not be possible to turn on Google Search without accepting AI.  

The company is updating its Search feature, so AI Overviews “will offer step-by-step guided learning” instead of instantly giving students the answers, but that does not offer comfort to the public.  

“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.” 

AI in schools has become a growing issue as parents and school leaders contemplate how to integrate a technology that is increasingly used in the workforce but viewed with extreme skepticism by critics.  

New York City is among multiple localities that has banned AI completely for younger students but still makes it available in some capacity for high schoolers. 

“It’s a small microcosm of the issue of AI in our world and AI in school districts, and then how school districts operate,” said Clay Lavercombe, freshman principal at Springboro High School in Ohio. 

“To change anything in the middle of a school year, big or small, I think is a challenge. I would hope that leaders would consider that, and maybe even Google would consider that — to allow school districts to determine what they want to do, but I’m sure that there’ll be some school districts, big and small, who say, ‘We cannot use Google, and we’ll have to figure something else out,'” he added.

But abandoning Google is not as simple as just switching search engines. An estimated 60,000 K-12 schools use Google Workplace, meaning teachers and students have integrated their work in Google emails, sheets and slides, according to Tech & Learning. Around 93 percent of U.S. public schools either use or plan on using Google Chromebooks in classrooms, About Chromebooks reported.

“I really think Google risks undermining its own position. They’ve had a tremendous amount of market share, but they’re ultimately forcing these schools and districts to choose between access to the information that they already have and controlling over how students use AI,” said Eric Gibbs, vice president of education at AI detection company Copyleaks, which works with schools around the country on AI usage.  

Google did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Advocacy groups had been pushing for the company to turn off its AI features on Google Search after discovering the platform would easily complete a homework assignment for students or give them all the answers. 

“We were really calling on Google to turn it off, recognizing that was probably the best way to ensure that kids were safe online and that we ensured that AI was not doing homework and schoolwork for kids,” said Yvette Renteria, chief programs officer at Common Sense Media. 

“And so, when Google puts out this choice of ‘You can only use Google Search with AI or you don’t use it at all,’ it’s really disturbing because, again, it takes away the opportunity to provide critical thinking skills, which is so important in education,” she added. 

A May 2026 Gallup poll said 50 percent of the U.S. workforce uses AI at least a few times a year and 15 percent uses the technology daily. That usage is expected to increase in the future.

Schools have tried several times to ban the technology due to cheating concerns, and some teachers have even switched assignments from online to in-person writing to avoid AI. 

AI supporters don’t think the fight is worth having.

The Google announcement “doesn’t bother me tremendously. I actually think AI is a useful tool. That, but we also have to have to teach our kids how to use AI. It’s a tool that has to be taught, similar to how to use safe internet practices or how to search on YouTube, use YouTube in appropriate ways. But it’s a tool that’s only going to get bigger, and … that genie’s not going back in the bottle,” said Dustin Strickland, an administrator at North Murray High School in Florida. 

“AI is here. It’s part of what is going to be part of our students’ lives. So rather than burying our head in the sand, I think we have to learn, have to teach our kids how to use it effectively,” he added.

data.title: Trump sends 'clear message' to Democrats with Miller promotion
data.description:
President Trump sent a blunt message to the incoming Democratic majority on Capitol Hill by tapping Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff, setting up what is likely to be a contentious two years between both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue. 

Miller is loathed by most Democrats, many of whom view him as xenophobic and racist. Additionally, the incoming chief of staff is not known to compromise with the other side of the aisle, preferring a combative approach to pushing the Trump agenda. 

Many see the move as Trump signaling to congressional Democrats that he is not thinking about compromise and will implement his agenda through executive authority.

“They are not going to slow down on executive power, executive orders, and regulations,” said Joe Grogan, former director of Trump’s Domestic Policy Council in his first administration and senior adviser at Covington & Burling LLP. “Stephen is going to move aggressively on all of that.”

Mick Mulvaney, who was Trump’s chief of staff during his first term, said the president’s pick of Miller sends “a clear message.” 

“The White House will continue to prioritize executive authority in the next two years,” Mulvaney told The Hill. 

“Stephen is a good choice on many levels, but face it, if the president was looking to build bridges with the new incoming Democrat majorities, he would probably have gone in a different direction,” he continued. 

Not everyone in Trump’s orbit and the broader GOP universe is thrilled about the decision. 

“We’re cooked,” said one former Trump administration official. “It’s exactly the opposite direction voters are begging Republicans to go. Susie was the best thing that happened to President Trump,” the former official continued, referencing chief of staff Susie Wiles, who resigned Friday. 

Another former Trump White House official who worked with Miller described the incoming chief of staff as “smart and opinionated, but does not have many close friends on the White House staff.” 

“Most of his colleagues view him as somewhat of an arrogant lone wolf,” the former official said.

“Trump likes him because he’s been a hard-liner on immigration enforcement in both his terms, but Trump has also gone against Miller when his ‘no holds barred’ approach goes too far like in Minneapolis earlier this year,” they added. 

The violent optics of the clashes between federal immigration enforcement and protesters in Minnesota earlier this year led, in part, to the ouster of former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Border Patrol officer Gregory Bovino, who served as commander at large of the law enforcement arm, was also removed from his position following the unrest. 

However, Miller, who strongly defended the operation, kept his role in the administration. 

His promotion comes after the president said Wednesday that he would “probably get along with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, adding that he wields “the power of the veto.” 

“They’ve already called, and they want to talk about things, and that’s fine,” the president said. 

Democrats, however, say Trump’s promotion of Miller has thrown that possibility out the window. 

“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a post on the social platform X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.” 

“Fire him today,” added Jeffries, who is likely to be the next House Speaker.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) responded to Miller’s promotion by saying Trump has “learned nothing from his historic defeat.” 

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” Schumer wrote on X. “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.” 

One Republican lobbyist warned the move to promote Miller will only worsen relations between the White House and Capitol Hill. 

“The president has two directions, one was to work with the Democratic Congress to try to get some things done. The other is to go to war with them. Stephen is more of a go-to-war guy,” the lobbyist said. 

But Grogan argued that Trump’s move to tap Miller as his chief of staff could be seen as a negotiating tactic in itself. 

“Trump is a negotiator and by picking Miller he is negotiating because he’s projecting strength, not weakness,” Grogan said.

data.title: Tillis says Miller is 'worst of all possible choices' for chief of staff role
data.description:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) blasted President Trump’s Friday decision to replace outgoing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with top adviser Stephen Miller, saying the president “needs to rethink” his decision.

“I’ve criticized a lot of the president’s advisors for bad advice that I think … created some of the environment on Tuesday, but the president made this decision, and the president needs to rethink it,” Tillis told CNN’s Jake Tapper Friday. 

“It is a colossal mistake, and the last thing we need 72 hours after the a– whooping we got on Tuesday,” he added.

Wiles’s replacement is the first major White House shakeup since Republicans’ rocky midterm performance, losing at least seven Senate seats and 42 House seats as of Friday — with several races still outstanding.

Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement tactics, which Miller architected, contributed to the president’s approval rating hitting a career low ahead of Election Day — likely impacting the GOP’s performance. One especially contentious operation at the start of 2026 took place in Minneapolis, during which two U.S. citizens were fatally shot by federal agents. At the time, Miller referred to the victims as domestic terrorists. 

“This past Tuesday, Republicans lost because we lost the narrative on the border, a success that the president should have been heralding,” Tillis said. “Now we’re talking about putting one of the most partisan, polarizing figures, and not only polarizing in terms of Republicans and Democrats, but even among Republicans.”

Just after the election night, Trump reportedly told aides Miller’s immigration campaign had gone too far, according to The Wall Street Journal. Tillis said it “doesn’t make sense” why Trump would promote Miller if he thought immigration had become a political liability.

“What was inappropriate is to take a guy who made us lose on the immigration issue,” Tillis said. “So no, he doesn’t get a passing grade for me, even judging on the kind of curve that I made with some people among his advisers.”

The GOP senator is frequent critic of some of Trump’s cabinet and other advisers. In March, he erupted at then Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in hearing, saying he was “disappointed” in her job performance.

In a viral post back in January, Tillis also compared Noem and Miller to “sycophants.”

The North Carolina Republican announced he would not run for reelection this year, and Gov. Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) won the open seat to replace him by nearly 20 points. The blue wave hit the Tar Heel State as hard as any Tuesday night; Democrats flipped five of its congressional seats, with five races still outstanding, according to Decision Desk HQ.

data.title: Former GOP governor: 'Wisconsin is a blue state'
data.description:
Former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson (R) declared the Badger State blue in a post-election interview Wednesday, pointing to recent statewide defeats for the GOP — including in its gubernatorial race.

“Wisconsin is no longer a purple state,” Thompson told Wisconsin Public Radio. “We haven’t won a statewide race for a long time. Wisconsin is a blue state, and it was before I got elected governor. And it’s gone back to that.”

Thompson was first elected in 1986 and served for four terms — making him the longest-serving governor in the state’s history. While the former governor won his race by wide margins, this year’s GOP candidate, Rep. Tom Tiffany, lost the race to Democrat David Crowley by 8 points on election night.

Republicans have won statewide races in Wisconsin in recent years — notably President Trump’s wins in 2016 and 2018 as well as Sen. Ron Johnson’s 2016 and 2022 victories. Thompson wrote the GOP’s recent success off as an anomaly, pointing to races for state supreme court that conservative-aligned candidates lost by wide margins.

“Trump was an aberration, but Wisconsin is still a blue state,” Thompson said. “You guys have got to realize that. And nobody can convince me this is a purple state anymore when you lose the supreme court justices by 15, 20 percent … and you lose the governorship by 8 points.”2

A conservative-aligned justice has not won election to the Wisconsin Supreme Court since 2019, and liberal-aligned candidates have claimed clear victories in 2020, 2023, 2025 and, most recently, a 20-point victory in 2026. In some cases, the races have received outsized attention, such as when Elon Musk poured $25 million into the contest in 2025 to support conservative candidates, but liberal-leaning Susan Crawford ended up winning by 10 points.

Though Wisconsin’s presidential races have remained close. Excluding former President Obama’s two races, where he carried the state easily, no presidential candidate has received a majority of the vote while winning Wisconsin since Michael Dukakis in 1988. In the last three presidential elections, the winning candidate claimed victory by less than one point.

Going forward, Thompson said the GOP needs to “rebuild,” arguing state Republicans have ignored Dane County — which includes the state’s capital, Madison — and Milwaukee County, two of the most populous and bluest counties in the state.

“I probably am the only Republican that’s ever carried Dane County when I was governor, and I carried Milwaukee County twice. And that’s because I spent a heck of a lot of time there,” Thompson said.

“If you want to overlook these counties you’re never gonna win,” he added. “Simple as that.”

data.title: DOJ dismisses lawsuit over California's 20,000 disputed ballots
data.description:
The Justice Department (DOJ) requested Friday to dismiss its lawsuit against California, which sought to make the state’s election officials set aside roughly 20,000 ballots for voters the federal government alleged were not U.S. citizens.

The Supreme Court already ruled against the Trump administration in an emergency order ahead of Election Day, preventing them from forcing California to set aside the ballots. A federal judge had previously blocked the administration’s request.

The DOJ had sought to prevent the state from counting the ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified.

The motion comes after Republicans faced sweeping losses in Tuesday’s midterms, during which they lost at least seven Senate and 42 House seats — and more races still outstanding.

The DOJ’s California lawsuit was one of several the agency brought forth ahead of Election Day. The Trump administration had also filed a lawsuit in Alaska seeking to block the state’s election certification if incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) lost, arguing the presence of another candidate on the ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., could have confused voters.

A judge dismissed that lawsuit before Election Day, but the Trump administration vowed to appeal. As of Friday, Sullivan narrowly trails his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola, in the Senate race — but no winner has been projected, as thousands of votes remain uncounted.

Accusations of noncitizen voting are not new for the Trump administration, which has sent threatening letters to state election officials and demanded states turn over their voter rolls to identify non-U.S. citizens.

Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Nevada of having nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens on its voter rolls. DHS later revised that number down to 185, but when Nevada officials investigated, they found all of those identified were actually U.S. citizens, The New York Times reported.

Noncitizen voting is permitted in some local elections but is illegal federally. Multiple studies have found that noncitizen voting is not widespread in U.S. elections.

On Election Day, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened any noncitizens who tried to vote with a warning.

“If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, [DHS] will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” Mullin wrote on social platform X.

data.title: California rejects billionaire tax proposal in win for executives, Newsom
data.description:
California voters are rejecting a proposal to impose a wealth tax on billionaire residents, marking a major win for tech and business executives, who spent hundreds of millions against the measure, according to a projection from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

According to DDHQ’s analysis, 54 percent voted against the measure, while 46 percent voted for it, with 76 percent of the total counted as of 8:51 p.m. EST.

Proposition 40 would have instituted a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth in a nationwide first. The government revenue from the wealth tax would have largely gone to state healthcare programs, with the remainder going to food assistance and education initiatives.

Preelection polling showed more California voters opposed the proposal, though the projections were tight.

The wealth tax proposal split California Democrats. The state Democratic Party and AFL-CIO and Teamsters unions supported the proposition, while Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) came out against it.

The term-limited governor said he supports a federal billionaire tax but took issue with the proposal dedicating “almost all of the revenue” from the tax to healthcare.

“There is nothing for housing, nothing for childcare, nothing for public safety workers who must answer 911 calls, and nothing for our public universities that have powered California’s economy for a decade,” Newsom wrote in a Substack post in June, adding, “This is not how we should set California’s budget priorities.”

California billionaires, including many Silicon Valley executives, lobbied against the measure, giving more than $333 million to the nonprofit Building a Better California.

An analysis from the nonpartisan state Legislative Analyst’s Office found California would have collected tens of billions of dollars by imposing the tax on the roughly 200 billionaires in the state.

The Hill’s Max Rego contributed.

data.title: Ex-RFK Jr adviser bashes White House on MAHA priorities
data.description:
Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., ripped outgoing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles over her tenure, arguing in a Friday interview she led the Trump administration to consistently bow to corporate interests when it came to health policy.

During a two-hour long Friday episode of “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Means detailed how Wiles and her allies — both inside and outside the White House — allegedly undermined what he said were politically popular efforts to improve Americans’ health, like regulating kratom, flavored e-cigarettes and sugary beverages.

Means, a Kennedy ally who helped build the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, resigned from the administration two weeks ago after clashing with the White House and becoming frustrated over the lack of progress on key MAHA priorities.

“The simple reality in why I left is that there is a very concentrated group of people in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for and are, frankly — I think it’s very clear — doing things for other reasons,” Means told Rogan.

The former Health and Human Services (HHS) official said Wiles, in particular, was laser focused on making sure special interests were contributing financially to both the administration and the GOP so they could have a monetary advantage in the midterms.

“Susie said to me many times, ‘We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms,’” Means said.

He also claimed Wiles once told him directly, “I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms.”

Means told Rogan that Wiles essentially ran the White House, saying she had a “stranglehold on any policy decision.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment. 

Wiles was a lobbyist before joining the Trump administration, and Means said she spent her career taking money from the highest paying clients, including from the pharmaceutical and pesticide industries as well as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On Friday, President Trump announced Wiles would leave her post and longtime White House adviser Stephen Miller would replace her starting next week.

In a lengthy post to social platform X reacting to Wiles’s departure, Kennedy defended the administration’s efforts to date, saying in part he and Trump “intend to keep fighting until the American people—not corporate influence—drive our health policies.”

Means also criticized Wiles and the administration’s handling of issues crucial to the MAHA movement, including the pesticide glyphosate, a key ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup.

The Trump administration spurred significant MAHA outrage when it issued an executive order calling for “adequate supply” of glyphosate-based herbicides for national security reasons.

The order was issued in February, just before the Supreme Court was about to hear oral arguments in a case that would determine whether Bayer, the maker of Roundup, could receive immunity from lawsuits alleging the weedkiller caused cancer.

Means told Rogan that a Wiles staffer “sat me down, put the EO on the table and said it’s not up for discussion.”

He went on to allege Wiles called Kennedy’s office and said, “We’re not discussing this.”

Means also said current FDA commissioner nominee, Heidi Overton, worked with the Department of Justice to draft a legal argument about why the Supreme Court should take up Bayer’s case and limit its lawsuit liability for some pesticide-related health harms.

Ultimately, the Supreme Court took the case and sided with the pesticide companies.

The former Kennedy adviser also expressed frustration at the administration’s delays at defining   “ultra-processed food,” another key MAHA priority.

“The amount of vitriol and lobbying on this issue, just having a simple definition out, because the food companies don’t want people to know the truth,” he said.

The Hill’s Rachel Frazin contributing to this report.

data.title: Wahab beats fellow Democrat in heated race for Swalwell's House seat
data.description:
Rep. Aisha Wahab (D-Calif.) is projected to win a full term representing California’s 14th District after Tuesday’s rematch against fellow Democratic candidate Melissa Hernandez, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Wahab’s victory comes just months after she beat Hernandez in August in a special election to fill the seat vacated by former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.). The embattled lawmaker resigned in April amid sexual misconduct allegations, which he has denied.

The race became an expensive and increasingly bitter battle between the two Democrats, drawing millions in outside spending from groups — including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee seeking to influence the party’s direction.

DDHQ had rated the district as “safely Democratic” ahead of Election Day, though the forecast does not distinguish between the candidates.

Wahab, the first Afghan American elected to Congress, previously served in the California state Senate and on the Hayward City Council. She campaigned on housing affordability, public safety and her record in Sacramento, Calif.

Hernandez, the former mayor of the town of Dublin and Bay Area Rapid Transit board president, also emphasized public safety and the economy while questioning the other candidate’s record.

Their rivalry intensified during an October debate when Hernandez accused her opponent of communicating with the Taliban, which Wahab condemned as a racist attack. She later defended the rhetoric as merely criticism of her fellow Democrat’s position on diplomacy with Afghanistan.

Wahab secured high-profile endorsements from California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), as well as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), the California Democratic Party and several labor organizations.

The Big Story 

US measles status to go up for review

The U.S. and Mexico will meet with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) for a three-day closed door meeting next week to evaluate their respective measles elimination statuses in light of ongoing outbreaks. 

© Jessie Wardarski, Associated Press

In January, the U.S. met one of the key conditions for a country to lose its measles elimination status: one year of consistent disease transmission. 

 

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the government has confirmed over 5,000 measles cases this year and nearly 7,500 since the start of 2025. Eight measles-related deaths have been reported across three states in 2026, though the CDC is only recognizing four as of November.

 

Despite meeting PAHO’s condition, Trump health officials argued in January that 12 continuous months of transmission alone should not result in an automatic loss of measles eliminations status, saying the international organization should also consider whether an epidemic linkage through a common source exists between cases.

 

But former Louisiana Surgeon General Ralph Abraham, who briefly served as the CDC’s principal deputy director before resigning in February, opined at the time losing measles elimination status in the U.S. was “not really” a significant loss. 

 

Canada lost its measles elimination status late last year. 

 

The U.S. and Mexico were scheduled to attend a meeting with PAHO to review their measles elimination statuses in April, but it was pushed back to November — citing the need to complete “ongoing analysis.” 

 

In the time measles outbreaks began spreading across the country, the CDC went without a permanent director for roughly a year. Even after Erica Schwartz was sworn in as the agency’s director in August, communication regarding the measles outbreaks has been scant. 

 

And members of the Trump administration have continued to cast doubt on the safety and efficacy of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, with President Trump calling the combined shot “quite lethal” from the Oval Office in August.

 

At a September conference hosted by anti-vaccine group Children’s Health Defense, Kennedy compared a child dying from measles to one sustaining injuries from vaccines, saying that — while children who die of the virus “get headlines” — kids are also “damaged” by shots.

data.description:

The Big Story 

DC officials ask incoming Democratic governors to pull Guard troops

Washington, D.C., officials are calling on incoming Democratic governors in five states that flipped blue to recall their National Guard troops from the nation’s capital.

© J. Scott Applewhite, Associated Press

During a D.C. Council hearing on Thursday, council member Brooke Pinto (D) — the chair of the public safety committee — said she would soon send a letter on behalf of the council to ask the governors-elect in Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Texas to “immediately” withdraw their soldiers back to their states.

 

“It’s something they can do their first day in office,” she said.

 

“While we have asked all of the governors across the country in the past to pull back their troops, we’ve been met with a lot of resistance and a lot of governors who are following the lead from President Trump,” Pinto noted. “But we now have the opportunity, with Tuesday’s election results, to turn the tide of what we’re seeing in Washington, D.C., and to have some real accountability to the federal government.”

 

Some 3,100 National Guard troops are deployed in Washington as part of President Trump’s “Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful” mission, which was announced last summer.

 

Of that number, just fewer than 760 troops are part of the D.C. National Guard — which is controlled by the sitting president — and 2,341 have been sent to the city by states and territories, nearly all of which are currently controlled by Republican governors, according to the mission’s joint task force.

 

While Texas, Ohio and Nevada currently only have one or two guard troops sent from each of their states, Georgia and Iowa can make a far bigger dent if they pull their 514 and 110 troops, respectively.

 

Should Alaska also flip to a Democratic governor — the race has yet to be called but has former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) currently leading — it would mean an additional 34 guard members could be recalled.

 

That means a total of 662 troops could be recalled from D.C. on come January.
